question_text: A 72-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for a wellness visit. He says that he has been experiencing episodes of chest pain and lightheadedness. Approximately 1 week ago he fell to the ground after abruptly getting up from the bed. Prior to the fall, he felt lightheaded and his vision began to get blurry. According to his wife, he was unconscious for about 5 seconds and then spontaneously recovered fully. He experiences a pressure-like discomfort in his chest and lightheadedness with exertion. At times, he also experiences shortness of breath when climbing the stairs. Medical history is significant for hypertension and hypercholesterolemia. He does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. Cardiac auscultation demonstrates a systolic ejection murmur at the right upper border and a normal S1 and soft S2. Which of the following is most likely found in this patient?

                    ### Question
                    A 72-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for a wellness visit. He says that he has been experiencing episodes of chest pain and lightheadedness. Approximately 1 week ago he fell to the ground after abruptly getting up from the bed. Prior to the fall, he felt lightheaded and his vision began to get blurry. According to his wife, he was unconscious for about 5 seconds and then spontaneously recovered fully. He experiences a pressure-like discomfort in his chest and lightheadedness with exertion. At times, he also experiences shortness of breath when climbing the stairs. Medical history is significant for hypertension and hypercholesterolemia. He does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. Cardiac auscultation demonstrates a systolic ejection murmur at the right upper border and a normal S1 and soft S2. Which of the following is most likely found in this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Bicuspid aortic valve
opb. Decreased murmur intensity with squatting
opc. High bounding pulses
opd. Increased blood flow velocity through the aortic valve

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with symptoms and physical exam findings suggestive of aortic stenosis, characterized by a systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border. In older adults, aortic stenosis is often due to age-related calcific changes, but in younger patients or those with a history of early onset, a bicuspid aortic valve is a common cause. The evidence path supports the association between aortic stenosis and a bicuspid aortic valve. Increased blood flow velocity through the aortic valve is a hallmark of aortic stenosis, as the narrowed valve opening causes the heart to pump harder, increasing velocity. Decreased murmur intensity with squatting is consistent with aortic stenosis, as squatting increases venous return and peripheral resistance, reducing the gradient across the stenotic valve. High bounding pulses and pulsus paradoxus are not typically associated with aortic stenosis; high bounding pulses are more indicative of aortic regurgitation, and pulsus paradoxus is associated with conditions like cardiac tamponade. Therefore, the most likely finding in this patient is increased blood flow velocity through the aortic valve, consistent with aortic stenosis.
